venues.d: Vietnam's most extravagant address — a maximalist Italian-designed palace of marble, gilt and glass atop the Times Square tower.

venues.a: District 1 (Đồng Khởi) — opposite the Opera House
venues.d: French-colonial calm on Lam Son Square — the city's most quietly assured luxury house, facing the Opera House.
A 1930s Indochine dream — Art Deco interiors, a museum's worth of period art, and a glorious rooftop pool over the city.
The war-correspondents' hotel since 1959 — a genuine piece of Saigon history on Lam Son Square, with the legendary Saigon Saigon rooftop bar.
Parisian opulence on a bend of the Saigon River since 1925 — stained glass, chandeliers and a river-facing rooftop, the city's oldest grande dame.
A design-forward boutique that celebrates old Saigon — greenery, craft and a rooftop pool tucked just off Đồng Khởi.
A polished, well-placed French luxury tower on leafy Lê Duẩn — dependable service and a rooftop pool.
A well-run riverside tower with wide Saigon River views and a top-floor pool — comfortable and central.

venues.a: District 1 — Ton That Dam / old market lanes
venues.d: Vietnam's first Michelin star — chef Peter Cường Franklin reimagines street food as fine dining, most famously his caviar-topped bánh mì.
Creative European cooking with Vietnamese soul from an Australian-trained chef — the city's most exciting new tasting menu.

venues.a: District 1 (Đồng Khởi) — Hôtel des Arts Saigon
venues.d: Refined Cantonese with a heritage dim sum lunch — the most polished Chinese kitchen in the city, inside Hôtel des Arts.

venues.a: District 1 (Đồng Khởi) — Hôtel des Arts Saigon
venues.d: An intimate teppanyaki counter of Japanese precision and premium produce — one of the hardest seats in Saigon.
Vietnamese home cooking kept exact and unhurried — the family recipes of the south and centre, raised to a star.
Wood-fire, market-led cooking from a well-travelled kitchen — bright, generous plates and a buzzy room.
A modern Vietnamese 'drinking-food' bar — bold, snacky, cocktail-driven cooking that landed on the regional radar fast.
One of Saigon's most storied phở houses — a generous southern bowl piled with herbs, since decades back.
A single, perfect southern phở — clean broth, tender beef, no ceremony.
Beef noodle soup from a tucked-away alley since 1945 — and a famous flaky pâté chaud pastry alongside.
The city's most famous broken-rice plate — an outsized grilled pork chop over rice, exactly as Saigon likes it.
A tiny stall serving one of the city's best bún bò Huế — the spicy, lemongrass-rich beef noodle soup of central Vietnam.
Saigon's most famous bánh mì — a fully loaded cold-cuts-and-pâté baguette that draws a permanent queue.
Homestyle Vietnamese cooking in a restored old villa full of antiques — rustic, romantic and much-loved.
Refined, fully plant-based Vietnamese cooking in a calm garden setting — meat-free without compromise.

The 1960s modernist presidential palace whose gates a North Vietnamese tank crashed through on 30 April 1975, ending the war. Inside it is frozen in that decade: the president's office, the war-room maps, the rooftop helipad, and the eerie basement bunker of telex machines. A private guide makes the political geography legible for a multi-generation family, and the leafy grounds give the grandparents somewhere shaded to pause.

The city's most affecting museum, telling the war from the Vietnamese side through photography, captured aircraft and tanks in the courtyard, and unflinching galleries on Agent Orange. It is emotionally heavy and best approached with older children rather than the very young; a guide who can pace the visit and step outside when needed is worth arranging.

A gloriously preserved 1890s beaux-arts hall often attributed to the Gustave Eiffel era, with a vaulted iron-and-glass ceiling, antique wall maps of old Cochinchina, and a huge portrait of Ho Chi Minh at the far end. Still a working post office, so you can send a postcard from the very desks; five minutes on foot from the cathedral.

The twin red-brick spires facing the post office are the postcard image of colonial Saigon, built with materials shipped from France. A major restoration runs to around 2027, so the interior is closed to visitors and the towers are under scaffolding; admire and photograph the exterior only, and note Masses still continue for worshippers.

A jewel-box 1900 French opera house on Lam Son Square, its ornate facade flanked by the Continental and Caravelle hotels. The interior is best seen by booking the resident A O Show, a bamboo-and-acrobatics spectacle that tells rural Vietnamese life without a word of dialogue, making it an easy, elegant multi-generational evening.

venues.n: Nguyen Hue Walking Street & People's Committee
venues.d: A broad pedestrian boulevard running from the ochre, French-baroque People's Committee building (city hall, floodlit and photogenic at night, exterior only) down to the river, with a statue of Ho Chi Minh at the head. It comes alive in the cool of the evening with families, buskers and fountains; the natural place for a post-dinner stroll.

A nine-storey 1960s residential block on the walking street, every balcony now a different independent cafe, boutique or gallery, its facade a mosaic of signboards and fairy lights. Ride the tiny paid lift to the top and work your way down; a fashionable, very Instagrammable stop for younger travellers with a coffee at each landing.

The helipad-crowned lotus-bud tower that defined the skyline before Landmark 81; its 49th-floor Skydeck gives a compact, central 360-degree view over the river bend and the colonial core. Being downtown, it is the easiest sunset viewpoint to fold into a District 1 afternoon, and the cafe-bar floors let the family linger over the lights coming on.

Vietnam's tallest building at 461 metres, its bamboo-bundle silhouette rising over a riverside park. The observation floors near the summit deliver the highest view in the country, with a glass-edge deck and cafe; pair it with a walk in the landscaped park below. A driver is sensible as it sits across the river from the tourist core.

The clock-towered 1914 covered market at the heart of downtown, a dense warren of fabric, lacquerware, coffee, dried fruit and souvenir stalls where haggling is expected. Best in the cooler morning for the food aisles; a guide or driver keeps a large group together and steers you to the fixed-price textile and lacquer stalls for cleaner buying.

An elegant 1929 Indochinese-style pavilion inside the Botanical Gardens, holding Cham sculpture, Oc Eo antiquities, a preserved mummy and dynastic bronzes. Compact and calm, it pairs naturally with the neighbouring zoo and gardens for a family morning, and offers real depth on the civilisations that preceded French Saigon.

venues.n: Fine Arts Museum (Bao Tang My Thuat)
venues.d: A honey-coloured 1930s mansion of a wealthy Chinese merchant, complete with the city's oldest lift and stained glass, now hung with lacquer paintings, silk works and wartime art. As much a house-museum as a gallery, it is a quieter, more architectural stop for those who have had their fill of temples and markets.

venues.n: Ho Chi Minh City Museum (Gia Long Palace)
venues.d: A grand neoclassical 1885 palace, once a governor's residence and later a presidential refuge, its bunker tunnels still beneath. Galleries trace Saigon's social history, and its gardens are a favourite for local wedding photography. A short, air-conditioned counterpoint a block from the cathedral and post office.

The most atmospheric Taoist temple in the city, built by the Cantonese community in 1909, thick with incense, carved wooden deities and a hall of the twelve midwives where couples pray for children. Small, dim and intensely alive; go early morning, dress with shoulders and knees covered, and let a guide unpack the crowded symbolism. Admission is free.

The finest of Saigon's Chinese temples, dedicated to Mazu the sea goddess, its courtyard hung with vast spirals of coiled incense smoke and its roofline crowded with intricate ceramic figurines. The spiritual heart of Chinatown and a photographer's temple; combine with a wander through Cholon's old shophouse lanes.

The grand yellow, pagoda-roofed wholesale market anchoring Cholon, Saigon's centuries-old Chinese quarter of herbalists, temples and gold shops. Less polished and more working than Ben Thanh, it rewards the curious traveller who wants the city's trading soul; a driver makes the run out from District 1 painless.

venues.a: Saigon River (boarding Bach Dang Pier / Nha Rong)
venues.d: An evening on the water with a buffet and live music as the illuminated Bitexco and Landmark 81 slide past; a relaxed, low-effort way to end a day for a group of mixed ages. Private charters can arrange a proper set menu with vegetarian courses on request rather than the standard buffet.

The vast network of hand-dug Viet Cong tunnels where families lived, cooked and fought underground; you can crawl a widened, lit section and see the camouflaged trap doors and living quarters. A powerful half-day for older children and history-minded travellers; a private car and guide beat the packed group buses, and the Ben Duoc entrance is quieter than Ben Dinh.

venues.n: Cao Dai Holy See, Tay Ninh
venues.d: The dazzling cathedral of Caodaism, Vietnam's home-grown faith blending Buddhism, Catholicism, Taoism and more, its nave a riot of dragon-wrapped pillars and a divine all-seeing eye. Time the visit for the noon ceremony, when white-, yellow- and blue-robed adherents fill the hall in silent ranks; galleries above let visitors watch respectfully. Often paired with Cu Chi or Ba Den.

venues.n: Cai Rang floating market & Can Tho
venues.a: Mekong Delta (Can Tho, ~3.5-4 hours south; overnight recommended)
venues.d: The delta's largest floating market, where wholesalers hoist samples of produce on tall poles above their laden boats at dawn. Because it peaks early, it rewards an overnight in Can Tho and a pre-sunrise boat; the real, working delta rather than the day-tripper version, best done unhurried with a private guide.

The leafiest slice of central Saigon, of tamarind-lined boulevards, French villas, the pink Tan Dinh Church and quiet specialty cafes. A neighbourhood for a slow guided walk rather than a checklist of sights, giving a sense of how the city's professional and old-money families actually live.

Coffee is Saigon's daily ritual, from robusta dripped over condensed milk (ca phe sua da) to the whipped egg coffee and the modern coconut-coffee. Time is well spent letting a guide take you from a plastic-stool pavement stall to a hidden third-wave roaster; it is one of the most authentic and effortless ways into local life for the whole family.

Saigon's street kitchen is among Asia's finest: the crackling French-Vietnamese banh mi, pho, broken-rice com tam and the fresh spring rolls of the south. A vetted evening food walk with a private guide can be routed to clean, trusted vendors and briefed in advance for vegetarian and Jain-friendly options, turning a daunting street scene into a highlight.

The city's loud, neon backpacker strip, a river of bars, street barbecue and music after dark. Not a luxury experience but a genuine slice of the city's nightlife energy, best sampled briefly and early from a quiet rooftop above the fray rather than in the thick of the crowd.

venues.n: Tao Dan Park & the bird-cafe scene
venues.d: A shaded downtown park where, in the early morning, locals bring caged songbirds to a corner cafe to sing together, alongside tai chi and badminton. A charming, free window into everyday Saigon life for early risers, a few minutes from the Reunification Palace.

venues.n: Xu Hoai / Ao Dai & lacquer artisan visits
venues.d: Saigon is the place to have a silk ao dai tailored within a day or two and to see traditional son mai lacquerware being layered and polished in small workshops. A private introduction to a trusted tailor or atelier turns shopping into a genuine craft experience and a lasting souvenir for the family.

Saigon does the sky-high sundowner beautifully, from long-running perches above Lam Son Square to sleek towers over the river. An elegant, air-conditioned way to watch the chaos of the streets resolve into a glittering skyline; the natural apertif before a river-view dinner.

The city now carries a serious high-end dining scene, from refined takes on regional Vietnamese cooking to internationally recognised tables. Worth booking ahead through a concierge, and easy to brief for vegetarian tasting menus; the leafy expat quarter of Thao Dien adds a relaxed, garden-restaurant option across the river.

venues.n: The colonial grand hotels (Continental, Majestic, Rex)
venues.d: A trio of legends: the Continental of Graham Greene's Quiet American, the riverfront art-deco Majestic, and the Rex with its wartime rooftop garden bar where correspondents once gathered. Even non-guests can take afternoon tea or a rooftop drink and step straight into old Saigon's story.

A vivid South-Indian temple to the goddess Mariamman, its gopuram crowded with painted deities, tucked among the downtown shophouses. For an Indian family it is a familiar and welcoming pause amid a very foreign city, and a reminder of Saigon's old Tamil trading community; a short walk from Ben Thanh Market.

One of the largest Buddhist pagodas in the city, its Japanese-influenced multi-storey tower and serene halls a calm counterpoint to the Chinese temples of Cholon. Spacious and uncrowded, it is an easy, dignified stop for a family and especially atmospheric around the lunar festivals.

An unexpectedly moving museum devoted to the women of southern Vietnam, their traditional dress, and their extraordinary role in the war. Small, well presented and rarely busy, it adds a human and gendered dimension to the harder-edged war narrative of the bigger museums.

A landmark 1960s concrete lotus-and-water roundabout that has become a beloved evening hangout for young Saigon, ringed by street-snack carts. Not a monument so much as a mood, best experienced at dusk with a fresh coconut or a plate of banh trang tron among the students.

One of the oldest zoos and botanical gardens in the world, a shaded green lung beside the History Museum with mature rain trees and orchid houses. A gentle option for families with younger children needing a break from museums and traffic, right in the centre of District 1.

A candy-pink, Romanesque-Gothic Catholic church from the 1870s that has become one of the city's most photographed facades. A quick, cheerful stop while exploring District 3, and a chance to see a working parish church while the more famous cathedral remains under restoration.

venues.n: Independence-era street art & the Post-Office lane cafes
venues.d: The lanes and hidden apartment-block cafes around the cathedral and post office hide a low-key creative scene of galleries, design shops and vintage stores. Worth an unhurried wander with a guide who knows which doorways open onto courtyards, for travellers who prefer texture over headline sights.

Beyond the tourist markets, the neighbourhood wet markets at dawn are where the city really shops, and the surrounding stalls serve the day's best pho. A private early walk here, followed by breakfast at a decades-old pho counter, is one of the most rewarding and grounding experiences the city offers.
Saigon's most celebrated cocktail bar — a hidden first-floor room reworking Vietnam's street drinks into precise, low-key cocktails.
Industrial-chic and inventive — cocktails built on local herbs and ingredients on the second floor of an old apartment block.
Artful cocktails and chilled vibes in a shabby-chic old colonial apartment — Summer Experiment's cooler big sister.
A playful, experimental cocktail den hidden in the same colonial block as Layla — one of Saigon's cult drinking rooms.
The war-correspondents' rooftop since 1959 — live music and a wraparound view over Lam Son Square and the Opera House.

venues.n: Social Club Rooftop Bar, Hôtel des Arts
venues.d: An infinity pool and one of the highest, most stylish rooftops in town — the District 3 skyline laid out below.
The city's original see-and-be-seen skybar — an open-air deck high over District 1 with a full skyline sweep.
Drinks near the top of Vietnam's tallest tower — the highest, most panoramic perch over the whole city and the Saigon River.
